scope: Quantitative island population and local-food pressure cases from Hawai'i, Samoa and Tahiti. These are validation-only: the records are contact-era or model/reconstruction estimates and do not provide an independently observed 1337 saturation fraction.

promotion_audit.decision: Do not promote. The cases are bounded islands with predominantly local food and useful density/pressure evidence, but the dated estimates are outside the 1337 window, use demographic or archaeological reconstruction, or have boundary/date uncertainty. Retain them as held-out global validation fixtures.

records.label: Tahiti pre-contact population and local-food pressure interval
pressure_evidence: Rallu's review of early navigator observations and demographic retrodictions places Tahiti at approximately 170,000-200,000 people in 1774 and 183,000-221,000 at 1767 contact; the 198,550 midpoint is the published reconstruction summarized by Sear et al. (2026), not a synthetic target.

Rallu documents a pre-contact high-density equilibrium in which fertility limitation/infanticide was used to stabilize population after centuries of growth. This is evidence of demographic pressure, not proof that the upper estimate equals biophysical carrying capacity.

The island is bounded and food production was overwhelmingly local: taro, breadfruit, banana, coconut, other Polynesian cultigens, pigs and near-shore fishing. Inter-island exchange is retained as a caveat rather than treated as imported staple calories.
The cited island area is approximately 1,045 km2, giving roughly 163-212 people per km2 across the retained interval; this is a useful density stress test for a high-productivity volcanic island.
records.trade_dependence: low_to_mixed; staple production was local, with inter-island exchange and chiefly redistribution
records.boundary_description: Entire Tahiti island in the Society Islands, French Polynesia; source area approximately 1,045 km2.
records.boundary_source: Rallu (2024), Tahiti Population (Re)Estimates and Ideologies, Population and Economics 8(2), pp. 231-262; Sear et al. (2026), Journal of Pacific Archaeology 16(2), Table A1.
records.source_family_independence: Published demographic reconstruction and independent Pacific-island synthesis; retained as one validation family and never used to set 1337 global scale.
records.notes: Rallu's upper contact estimates are historically plausible but debated. They are included to expose whether the physical model can represent a densely settled volcanic island, not as a two-sided Malthusian label. The EU5 Tahiti row has 1,041.129505 km2 versus the cited 1,045 km2; the 99.63% area coverage is explicitly recorded in the crosswalk.

records.label: Upolu, Samoa: pre-contact population reconstruction and drought-pressure interval
pressure_evidence: Sear et al. (2026), Table A1, reports a 109,000 genetic reconstruction for Samoa and 75,400 assigned to Upolu, with an Upolu area of 1,125 km2; Green's independent demographic estimate for the archipelago is 70,000.

The archaeological and palaeoclimate review describes permanent settlement, intensive horticulture and sensitivity of makatea/high-island food systems to drought. Population density and climate thresholds are retained as validation pressure evidence, not converted into a saturation fraction.

The island food regime was locally supplied by taro, breadfruit, banana, coconut, yam, pigs and fishing. The genetic estimate may describe effective or reconstructed population rather than a direct census, so the broad interval is retained.

Upolu is a bounded volcanic island and the EU5 named island row covers the cited area to within approximately one percent, allowing a useful held-out density comparison without redistributing an archipelago total.
records.trade_dependence: low_to_mixed; local horticulture and fishing supplied staples, with inter-island movement and chiefly redistribution
records.boundary_description: Entire Upolu island, Samoa; Sear et al. (2026) reports approximately 1,125 km2 and assigns a 75,400-person component of the Samoa reconstruction to Upolu.
records.boundary_source: Sear et al. (2026), Journal of Pacific Archaeology 16(2), Table A1 and pp. 17-19; Harris et al. (2020), PNAS 117, 31929-31935; Green (2002) demographic estimate as cited by Sear et al.
records.source_family_independence: Genetic reconstruction, demographic estimate and archaeological/climate synthesis are retained as one island validation family; they do not establish a 1337 target.
records.notes: The lower and central values are not interchangeable observations: 70,000 is an archipelago demographic estimate, 75,400 is the Upolu component of the genetic reconstruction, and 109,000 is the whole-Samoa genetic total. They are kept in one broad validation interval only to test sensitivity to reconstruction method. No value trains the model.

records.label: Hawai'i Island: pre-contact intensive agriculture and reconstructed population peak
pressure_evidence: Ladefoged et al. (2009) model 572 km2 of feasible intensive agriculture on Hawai'i Island, approximately 97% rain-fed dryland, with about 97,000 metric tons of potential crop production and 165,000 agricultural workers under the modeled system. These are independent agricultural-physics diagnostics, not a population target.

The same paper describes Hawai'i as isolated and bounded, with intensive pondfield and dryland systems built from locally available taro, sweet potato and other Polynesian cultigens. It reports a pre-contact archipelago population range of 200,000-800,000 and discusses land-base limits and ecosystem transformation.

Kirch's archaeological population synthesis, as reviewed in the Hawai'i archaeology literature, places a conservative island peak near 150,000 around the fifteenth century; the broad 100,000-200,000 interval is retained because island-level reconstruction is not a census and estimates vary materially.
The archaeological record of field-system expansion and later stabilization is a useful intensive/pressure case, but no independent saturation fraction is asserted.
records.trade_dependence: low_to_mixed; staple calories were local, with inter-island exchange and chiefly redistribution
records.boundary_description: Entire Hawai'i (Big Island) in the Hawaiian archipelago; published land area approximately 10,430 km2. The EU5 map has four named locations (Hilo, Kohala, Kona and Ka'u) covering a quantified partial footprint.
records.boundary_source: Ladefoged et al. (2009), Opportunities and Constraints for Intensive Agriculture in the Hawaiian Archipelago Prior to European Contact, Journal of Archaeological Science 36:2374-2383; Kirch (2007), Like Shoals of Fish: Archaeology and Population in Pre-Contact Hawai'i.
records.source_family_independence: GIS agricultural model and archaeological population synthesis are retained as one validation family; no scale or regional correction is inferred.
records.notes: The EU5 selector covers 8,521.049440 km2 against the published approximately 10,430 km2 island area (81.66%). It is deliberately not a training aggregate: population is reconstructed, the crosswalk is partial, and the agricultural production numbers are a separate physical validation of crop/land allocation.
